title_en: Fragment on the Gospel of Matthew
author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
occasion: A brief exposition of Matthew 6:22-23, explaining the saying about the eye as the lamp of the body in terms of sincere versus pretended love.
argument: Gregory interprets the 'simple eye' as unhypocritical love, through which the whole body is enlightened and a person's outward words match inward thoughts. The 'evil eye' is feigned love, also called hypocrisy, through which the whole body of the man is darkened. Such hypocrites inwardly devise deeds worthy of darkness while outwardly speaking words that seem full of light; they are truly wolves who have put on sheep's skins. They wash only the outside of the cup and dish, not knowing that unless the inside is cleansed, the outside cannot become clean. The Savior therefore convicts them by asking: if the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness? Gregory explains this means that if what you think is love is actually a work deserving darkness because of hidden hypocrisy, how much worse are your open transgressions?

outline.move: Quotes Matthew 6:22-23 and identifies the simple eye as unhypocritical love and the evil eye as pretended love or hypocrisy.

Describes hypocrites as inwardly devising deeds of darkness while outwardly speaking words that seem full of light; they are truly wolves in sheep's skins, and they wash only the outside of the cup and dish without knowing that the inside must first be cleansed.
Introduces the Savior's convicting question from Matthew 6:23: if the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness?
Explains the question: if your supposed love is really a work deserving darkness because of hidden hypocrisy, how much worse are your open sins?

Hypocrisy, the outward appearance of virtue concealing inward evil.

Sheepskins, the outward disguise worn by wolves, symbolizing false appearance of innocence.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὰ αὐτὰ τοῖς ἔσωθεν νοούμενοις, καὶ διὰ τῶν ἔξωθεν μερῶν προφέρουσα
_unresolved_facts.fix: the same things as the inward thoughts are brought forth through the outward parts

_unresolved_facts.claim: They wash only the outside of the cup and dish, not knowing that unless the inside is cleansed, the outside cannot become clean
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οἱ τὸ ἔξωθεν τοῦ ποτηρίου καὶ τῆς παροψίδος μόνον πλύνοντες, καὶ οὐκ εἰδότες, ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ τὸ ἔσωθεν τούτων καθαρισθῇ, οὐδὲ τὸ ἔξωθεν καθαρὸν δύναται γενέσθαι
_unresolved_facts.fix: They wash only the outside of the cup and the side-dish, not knowing that unless the inside of these is cleansed, the outside cannot become clean either

_unresolved_facts.claim: Describes hypocrites as inwardly devising deeds of darkness while outwardly speaking words that seem full of light; they are truly wolves in sheep's skins, and they wash only the outside of the cup and dish without knowing that the inside must first be cleansed
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἄξια μὲν σκότους πράγ-ματα ἐννοούμενον ἔσωθεν· διὰ δὲ τῶν ἔξωθεν μερῶν, φωτὸς εἶναι δοκοῦντα προφέρον ῥήματα
_unresolved_facts.fix: The participles ἐννοούμενον and προφέρον are singular, describing a single hypocrite (or the generic hypocrite), not plural 'hypocrites'

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Gospel text is quoted without an introductory formula, apparently as Gregory's own opening
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὁ λύχνος τοῦ σώματός ἐστιν ὁ ὀφθαλμός. Ἐὰν οὖν ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ἁπλοῦς ᾖ...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opening quotation lacks an introductory formula but is clearly scriptural citation (Matthew 6:22-23), not Gregory's own words; the voice shifts to Gregory's interpretation at 'Ἀπλοῦς ὀφθαλμός, ἡ ἀνυπόκριτός ἐστιν ἀγάπη'
